question.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ]\,,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)=k$ and $y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+k$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
question.worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }k(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+k)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(k\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+{k}^{2}t){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =k\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+{k}^{2}\pi -k\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-0 \\  & ={k}^{2}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}\pi  & =0 \\ k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
